triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: claimed wisdom and false handling of sacred writing
triples.rationale: Jeremiah challenges people claiming wisdom and possession of the Lord's law by naming a false reed-pen for scribes; the next unit says the wise rejected the Lord's word. Peter distinguishes Paul's given wisdom from the unlearned and unstable who distort his letters and the other Scriptures. Both deny that proximity to sacred writing guarantees faithful understanding. Peter does not identify Jeremiah's scribes, and Jeremiah's wording is not expanded into a description of a particular altered manuscript.
triples.source_text: How will you say, ‘We are wise, and the Lord’s law is with us’? A false reed-pen came to be in vain for scribes.

target_units.text: and consider the patience of our Lord to be salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him,

as also in all his letters, speaking in them about these things. In them are some things hard to understand, which the unlearned and unstable will distort, just as they will distort the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.
Therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, guard yourselves so that you are not carried away by the error of lawless people and fall from your own firm position.

triples.relationship: Prophetic sign parallel: a divinely assigned name declares judgment
triples.rationale: Jeremiah tells Pashhur that the Lord has named him Migrant, and immediately explains the migration and captivity awaiting him. The Lord commands Hosea to name his daughter Not Shown Mercy and explains the announced withholding of mercy from Israel's house. In both, a divinely assigned name embodies the following judgment. Pashhur is renamed as an adult while Hosea names a child; the distinct names and punishments are not equated.
triples.source_text: And Pashhur brought Jeremiah out of the trap, and Jeremiah said to him: The Lord has called your name not Pashhur but Migrant.

target_units.text: She conceived again and bore a daughter. He said to him, “Call her Not Shown Mercy, for I will certainly no longer show mercy to Israel’s house, but I will surely set Myself against them.

triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: successive bearers of war news reaching a king
triples.rationale: Jeremiah depicts pursuer meeting pursuer and announcer meeting announcer to report Babylon's capture to its king. Samuel describes Cushi and Ahimaaz carrying news from the fighting to David, with Ahimaaz overtaking Cushi and both reports reaching the king in succession. Both scenes convey a military outcome through multiple messengers to a ruler. David's battlefield victory and concern for his son differ from Babylon's captured city, and Jeremiah's pursuers are not identified with Samuel's runners.
triples.source_text: Pursuer will pursue to meet pursuer, and announcer to meet announcer, to tell Babylon’s king that his city has been captured;

target_units.text: Joab said to Cushi, “Go, report to the king everything you have seen.” Cushi bowed to Joab and went out.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke again to Joab: “Let me too run after Cushi.” Joab said, “Why are you running, my son? Come here. There is no news that will benefit you by going.”
He said, “What if I do run?” Joab told him, “Run.” Ahimaaz ran by the road of Kechar and overtook Cushi.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the gate roof by the wall, raised his eyes, and saw a man running alone before him.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, there is good news in his mouth.” The man kept coming nearer.
The watchman saw another man running. He called out by the gate, “There is another man running alone.” The king said, “He too brings good news.”
The watchman said, “I recognize the first man’s running: it is like Ahimaaz son of Zadok’s.” The king said, “He is a good man; he comes with good news.”
Ahimaaz called to the king, “Peace!” He bowed to the king with his face to the ground and said, “Blessed is the Lord your God, who has shut out the men who hated their hand against my lord the king.”
The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom well?” Ahimaaz said, “I saw a great crowd when Joab sent the king’s servant and your servant, but I did not know what was there.”
The king said, “Turn aside and stand here.” He turned aside and stood.
Then Cushi arrived and said to the king, “Let my lord the king receive good news: the Lord has vindicated you today against the hand of all who rose against you.”
The king asked Cushi, “Is the young man Absalom well?” Cushi said, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rose against him to do harm, be like that young man.”

triples.relationship: Narrative contrast: offered wine tests fidelity
triples.rationale: The Lord sends Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into a temple court and offer them wine; the surrounding account records their refusal because of their ancestor's command. Daniel's assigned royal provision includes wine, but he seeks to avoid its pollution and proposes a test using water and legumes, after which the wine is removed. Both accounts place offered wine against a commitment that leads to abstention. The temple demonstration of ancestral obedience differs from Daniel's royal-house food test and its stated concern about contamination.
triples.source_text: Go to the house of the Rechabites. Bring them into the Lord’s house, into one of the courts, and give them wine to drink.

target_units.text: and to give them a ration from the king’s house each day, from the royal table and the wine the king drank, and to educate them for three years and place some of them before the king.
Among the lineage of Israel’s sons from Judea were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
The chief eunuch assigned them names: Daniel, Baltasar; Hananiah, Sedrach; Mishael, Misach; and Azariah, Abdenago.
Daniel considered in his heart how he might avoid being polluted by the king’s dinner and the wine he drank, and petitioned the chief eunuch that he might not be contaminated.
The Lord gave Daniel honor and favor before the chief eunuch.

The chief eunuch said to Daniel, “I am anxious about my lord the king, who prescribed your food and drink, lest he see your faces drawn and weak beside the foreign youths being reared with you, and I risk my own neck.”
Daniel said to Abiesdri, appointed chief eunuch over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
“Test your servants for ten days, and let us be given legumes from the earth to eat, and water to drink.
If our appearance looks drawn beside the other young men eating the royal dinner, then deal with your servants however you wish.”
He dealt with them in this manner and tested them for ten days.
After ten days their appearance was good and their bodily condition better than the other young men eating the royal dinner.
Abiesdri kept removing their dinner and wine and giving them legumes in exchange.

triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: mass killing into a pit
triples.rationale: Jeremiah describes Ishmael slaughtering the arriving men into a cistern after inviting them into the city; the following explanation says that cistern was filled with the slain. Maccabees says Bacchides seized deserters and some of the people and slaughtered them into a great pit. The particular correspondence is killing a group into a cavity, not merely warfare or murder. The leaders, victims and occasions remain distinct, and the target's pit is not identified as Asa's cistern.
triples.source_text: When they entered the middle of the city, he slaughtered them into the cistern.

target_units.text: Bacchides withdrew from Jerusalem and encamped at Beth-zaith. He sent and seized many of the men who had deserted to him and some of the people, and slaughtered them into the great pit.

deferred_source_units.source_text: Therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep became sweet to me.
deferred_source_units.reason: The newly read Proverbs passage promises pleasant sleep with confident safety, whereas this source reports awakening and sweet sleep after a restoration oracle. The common favorable-sleep description does not establish a sufficiently particular additional relationship for this source; it remains pending and its original deferral is preserved.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep became sweet to me.
unresolved_candidates.reason: Proverbs links pleasant sleep to fearlessness and the Lord’s protection on one’s ways. Jeremiah records an awakening and sweet sleep after the preceding oracle. The positive description of sleep alone is too general to establish a particular prophetic or narrative correspondence; no pair is retained.

target_units.text: For if you sit, you will be fearless, and if you sleep, you will sleep pleasantly.
You will not fear an approaching fright or the oncoming assaults of the ungodly,
for the Lord will be upon all your ways and support your foot so that you are not shaken.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: When they entered the middle of the city, he slaughtered them into the cistern.
unresolved_candidates.reason: The actual Kings passage describes Jehu killing Ahaziah’s brothers at Baithakad, but does not state that they were killed into a pit or cistern. The anticipated shared disposal detail is absent. This proposal remains unretained; the distinct Maccabees passage supplies an actually read slaughter-into-a-pit comparison.

target_units.text: and Jehu found the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah. He said, ‘Who are you?’ They said, ‘We are Ahaziah’s brothers, and we have come down for the peace of the king’s sons and the ruling lady’s sons.’
He said, ‘Seize them alive.’ They seized them alive and slaughtered them at Baithakad, forty-two men. He left not one of them.
